prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for base editing to Liu, Komor and Gaudelli. After round 1 the case rests on three points I can check against what I know of nucleotide chemistry. First, the chemistry is defined and distinct from cleavage: a deaminase converts cytosine to uracil, or an evolved TadA converts adenine to inosine, on DNA, which is a substrate these enzymes do not act on in nature. Second, the two editor classes are separate inventions. The cytosine editor needed the uracil glycosylase inhibitor and nickase-directed strand choice to bias the cell's repair, and the adenine editor needed directed evolution of TadA to work on DNA at all. This is why a Liu-only citation would hide half the achievement and why Komor and Gaudelli each carry a seat. Third, independent laboratories have reproduced and extended both editors, and patients have been treated. The remaining objections, the 2020 prize, Target-AID and clinical maturity, are real, but round 1 showed that the main rival, B011, carries the same maturity objection (no approved degrader) and a harder attribution cut, so I do not see a reason to move.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against my own position is that base editing arrives six years after the CRISPR prize and may be read as the next step in one genome-editing story. The clinical record is short, and long-term safety, bystander edits and off-target deamination, including RNA and genome-wide deaminase activity, are still being characterised. Attribution also remains open: Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID is a genuine parallel cytidine-editor result, the three-name limit excludes them for reasons of space and not of merit, and a committee that treats priority for the cytosine editor as unresolved would have a weaker citation. There is also a legitimate argument that waiting for the first approved base-editing therapy would make the prize safer.

responses.point: Johan accepts that base editing is a serious alternative but says he cannot count the short clinical record against PROTACs and not against base editing, and he is uncomfortable with the three-seat attribution given Kondo and Nishida.
responses.response: I agree with the symmetry on maturity and I said so in round 1: neither field has an approved product that I am aware of, so timing does not separate B007 from B011. Where I differ is on what then decides. For B011 the committee must choose three from Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli, Handa, Ito and Gray and has to decide whether bifunctional degraders and cereblon glues are one achievement, which you and Daniel both flag as unresolved. For B007 the cut is Target-AID versus the trio, and Target-AID covers only the cytidine editor, so the adenine editor and the shared concept remain cleanly attributable. A narrower, cleaner attribution at equal maturity is, for me, the tiebreaker, and your point on breadth of ranking does not change that because breadth does not tell us who deserves the credit.

responses.point: Heiner agrees on the trio and presses me to be precise about the dates of Target-AID against Komor et al. 2016, and to word the citation around the chemistry of base conversion and state openly that the three-name limit, not merit, excludes Kondo and Nishida.
responses.response: I accept both requests. My recollection, which I cannot verify from the shortlist alone, is that the Komor et al. cytosine base editor and the Nishida et al. Target-AID paper appeared within a few months of each other in 2016 and that the work was independent, so I would not claim priority on dates and would not ask the committee to. That is why I have reworded the citation around the chemical conversion of single bases and not around one laboratory. I would also be content for the expert report to say plainly that Kondo and Nishida are excluded by the limit. Where I hold my position is on the adenine editor, which has no Target-AID counterpart and is the strongest reason the prize should name Gaudelli.

responses.point: Peter proposes a two-part prize, Pd-catalysed C-N coupling for Buchwald and Hartwig plus base editing for Liu alone, and concedes the two parts have no common theme and that B065 had thin support.
responses.response: I take the two-part idea seriously, and your concession about thin support for B065 is honest. But I would not take base editing as a Liu-only second part. The two editors are chemically different inventions with different enzymes, and naming only the group leader would credit the idea and not the deaminase engineering, which is the chemistry we are being asked to honour. Your pairing also needs three people in total, which forces Liu alone, and I would sooner keep a single, explainable base-editing prize with three names than split it to make room for a part that seven of us ranked low or not at all.

responses.point: Peter asks what chemical principle in base editing is new beyond fusing a known enzyme class to a programmable targeting module, and wants priority and off-target safety examined before B007 is a first choice.
responses.response: The new principle is not the fusion itself. It is making a nucleotide-modifying deaminase act on genomic DNA at a single defined base, and arranging that the cell's own repair converts the edit into a permanent change: uracil glycosylase inhibition and strand-directed nicking for the cytosine editor, and an evolved TadA for adenine, since no natural enzyme deaminates adenine in DNA. That is protein evolution and mechanism-based design, not simply bolting two parts together, and it is why I call it chemistry. On safety, I agree it is incompletely closed, and I would put it in the expert report; I do not think it changes the maturity ranking against B011 or B028, where the open points are larger. I will also add that nitrogenase remains a strong alternative from my side only if the committee finds the N2 binding mode less decisive than I do.

responses.point: Xiaodong says naming two trainees alongside the principal investigator would be unusual and expects some members to see base editing as an extension of CRISPR, which she regards as a reasonable perception.
responses.response: I agree that the perception is reasonable and that is why I list it as the strongest argument against my position. My answer is that the 2020 prize honoured programmable cleavage and the chemistry of RNA-guided DNA cutting, whereas base editing is a different reaction that avoids cutting and was only possible because of deaminase engineering. On the trainees, I weigh who made the decisive invention and not seniority: Komor and Gaudelli were the first authors of the two founding editors and each editor class stands on their work. If the committee is unwilling to credit them, the honest alternative is another candidate, not a Liu-only base-editing citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges base editing distinct enough from the 2020 CRISPR prize and far enough after it
Whether the exact priority of Target-AID relative to the cytosine base editor is independently established, since my recollection of the dates is not verified
Whether long-term off-target and bystander safety will change the clinical picture before the committee must decide
Whether B011 becomes the stronger choice if an approved degrader exists and the committee can define a clean three-name cut between bifunctional degraders and cereblon glues
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict. My research on dNTP pools and replication fidelity is topically adjacent to DNA editing and nucleotide chemistry, but I have no personal, institutional or collaborative connection to any base-editing, degrader or lipid nanoparticle candidate, and my view is unchanged from round 1.
